newsitem.title: SPAIN: FORECAST - Spain 1996-end CPI seen tame, under goal.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Spain 1996-end CPI seen tame, under goal.

text.p: Spanish inflation, widely expected to end 1996 at a tame 3.2 percent, will not prod the Bank of Spain into a sharp interest rate cut, analysts said on Monday.

Analysts said CPI will undershoot its official 1996 target of 3.4 percent, and Spain's central bank is likely to shrug aside Wednesday's data and wait for the January consumer price index, which could provide the go-ahead for aggressive reductions in the 6.25-percent official rate.

But analysts admitted that the peseta's recent strength has tempered this outlook and may force the Bank of Spain to ease into the rate cut mode with a small reduction as soon as next Thursday's regular repurchase operation.
"They already have room to cut around 25 bps but for a more aggressive rate cut, they'll wait for more CPI data," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
According to a Reuter survey of economists, Spanish CPI is seen having risen 0.28 percent in December, for a year-on-year inflation rate of 3.2 percent.
In November, CPI was unchanged month-on-month for a 3.2 percent yearly rise, down from 3.5 percent in October.
But analysts said the markets and the Bank of Spain had already widely discounted the 1996 moderation and were now looking ahead to a more difficult test - the January data.
Prices from petrol to consumer oil have risen this month. The first month of the year is usually considered a hot month for inflation, analysts said.
In January 1996, Spanish inflation rose 0.6 percent month-on-month in the general index and 0.5 percent in the core.
"They'll wait for the January data, which is really difficult to forecast. The only thing that could force the Bank of Spain to an early move is the peseta's strength," she said.
On Friday, the peseta broke through 84.00 versus the mark, to reach the highest level since May.
At 1400 GMT, the Spanish currency was at 83.40/3.42 versus the mark after touching a low at 83.35.
And the market was pushing short-term interest rates lower, with one-year bill yields below 5.50 percent, and steepening the yield curve.
"The market's really aggressive. If you look at short-term futures contracts, they are factoring in an official rate of around five percent by September," said Urrutia.
The Bank of Spain had cut its official repurchase rate to 6.25 percent at the end of 1996 from nine percent in January.
"Recent declarations (by the central bank) suggest the Bank of Spain will be unlikely to pursue as aggressive monetary policy easing as in 1996," Banco SanPaolo in London wrote on Monday.
But they added that there still remains room for one more cut by the end of the first quarter if, as expected, inflation falls below three percent year-on-year in the first three months.
